tagline: Farmland, maple work and river crossings on the way to Canada
intro: The Maple Traditions Scenic Byway runs 80 miles from Lowville through farmland and woodland to the foot of the international bridge at Ogdensburg. New York State DOT identifies scenic and historic themes, emphasizing food and crafts made from the land and access to woods, fields and waterways. Family sugar bushes produce maple syrup with wood-stoked fires and horse-drawn wagons; Amish farmers work the fields.

The numbered highway took shape through a campaign to simplify a much longer journey. In 1975, regional DOT officials proposed NY 812 as part of a plan to connect Deposit on the Delaware River with the international bridge using as few route numbers as possible. Implemented on July 1, 1977, NY 812 replaced NY 87 and the Lowville–Croghan portion of NY 26A. New York took over maintenance of the Croghan–Harrisville segment in 1980 and the Harrisville–Fowler section in 1982.

From Lowville, NY 812 follows the Black River briefly before crossing into New Bremen and continuing to Croghan. Northward come Harrisville, Gouverneur and De Kalb, then Heuvelton on the Oswegatchie and Ogdensburg at the St. Lawrence. An alternate loop through Canton passes the North Country Heritage Center, with exhibits and archives devoted to regional customs and folk arts.

moments.title: Croghan
moments.text: The American Maple Museum occupies a school financed by a logging fortune. Theodore B. Basselin became Croghan’s first millionaire through his logging business and was one of its leading employers. His estate paid for the Father Leo Memorial School, now the museum beside St. Stephen’s church. Other buildings carry his story through the village: the Basselin mansion stands downtown, and the library down the road was once his opera house. The Basselin Cemetery is next to the library. Croghan is locally pronounced Krō-gun, with a hard g and a silent h.

moments.title: Heuvelton
moments.text: NY 812 becomes State Street through Heuvelton, where it crosses the Oswegatchie River. The settlement was first called Fordsburgh and also went by East Branch, a name tied to the river. In 1832 it took the name of Jacob Van den Heuvel, an immigrant from the Netherlands whose investments included mills. Another chapter occupies three floors of stone at Pickens Hall, built in 1858. The building entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2004. Its third-floor opera house has been restored as a performance venue, above a general store and second-floor function space.

moments.title: Ogdensburg–Prescott International Bridge
moments.text: The byway ends at the foot of a suspension bridge completed in 1960. Despite its name, the Canadian landing is at Johnstown, east of Prescott. The name recalls the ferry service between Ogdensburg and Prescott that the bridge was intended to replace. Vessels had crossed between those communities since 1800; an international rail ferry also carried rail cars across from 1858 to 1970. The American approach carries NY 812; the Canadian connection is Highway 16. Designed by Modjeski & Masters, the bridge has six spans extending 1.5 miles across the St. Lawrence River and Seaway.
